source_records.title: Privacy-Preserving, Decentralised Inference of Epidemic Transmission Dynamics from Digital Exposure Histories
source_records.abstract: BackgroundExposure-history data collected during epidemics or pandemics within digital contact-tracing applications hold immense potential for rapid, scalable epidemiological inference. The sensitivity of these data makes privacy-preserving designs essential to secure public trust and app uptake. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, such approaches were not yet available at the scale or maturity required for deployment. We present a Bayesian decentralised framework to infer transmission dynamics from exposure-history data while protecting user privacy. MethodsOur approach is based on iterative communication between user devices and a central server, computing log-likelihood gradients on device from exposure-history data and centrally updating parameter values using only aggregated gradients. Applying this framework to synthetic exposure-history data from a hypothetical respiratory pathogen epidemic simulated on dynamic contact networks, we assessed its ability to estimate the underlying transmission parameters, perform infector attribution, and reconstruct serial-interval (SI) distributions. We systematically explored how inference was affected by incomplete exposure-history data arising from partial app adoption, case under-ascertainment, and incomplete exposure logging, and by transmission scenarios. FindingsOur decentralised framework accurately recovered transmission parameters, closely matching estimates derived from centralised data with no systematic bias in posterior means. Parameter recovery remained robust when hazards from unobserved exposures were known as a daily average across the population. Although incomplete exposure-history data and specific transmission scenarios introduced compensatory parameter biases, the inferred host infectiousness profile retained sufficient accuracy, and the weekly SI distributions reconstructed from infector attributions closely resembled the ground-truth distributions. InterpretationOur findings highlight that, beyond its primary role as a control measure, digital contact tracing could help characterise transmission dynamics almost in real time and inform public health interventions while preserving user privacy. FundingOxford Martin School Programme on Digital Pandemic Preparedness; National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Protection Research Unit in Emerging and Zoonotic Infections. Evidence before this studyWe searched PubMed for studies published from database inception to Sept 30, 2026, using the keywords ("digital contact tracing" OR "exposure notification" OR "contact tracing app") AND ("federated learning" OR "decentralised" OR "privacy-preserving" OR "statistical inference" OR "Bayesian inference") AND ("transmission" OR "serial interval" OR "infectiousness"). During the COVID-19 pandemic, digital contact-tracing (DCT) apps were deployed at an unprecedented scale: 224 COVID-19 apps were launched across 127 countries, 128 of which supported exposure notification. In England and Wales, the NHS COVID-19 app had 16.5 million regular users (28% of the total population) and averted an estimated 1 million cases and 9,600 deaths in its first year. To protect privacy, however, most apps used decentralised architectures that kept exposure-history data on users devices. This privacy-preserving principle has largely prevented these data from being used for epidemiological inference to understand transmission dynamics, such as estimating the serial-interval (SI) distribution and host infectiousness profile over time. While existing decentralised algorithms estimate each users infection risk, we found no study that developed and evaluated a framework for estimating population-level epidemiological parameters from exposure-history data that remain on users devices. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first such framework. It estimates key quantities required for understanding transmission dynamics, including how an infected individuals infectiousness changes over time relative to their symptom onset date, how much close contacts increase the risk of transmission, and the SI distribution. The framework learns an exposure hazard function from data that never leave users devices, then attributes infections to likely infectors, and reconstructs the SI distribution. We applied the framework to synthetic exposure-history data from epidemics simulated on dynamic contact networks of 166,034 individuals, matching the 2024 population of Oxford, UK. It produced estimates comparable to those from centralised analysis, identified the timing of peak host infectiousness relative to symptom onset to within one day, and reconstructed SI distributions that closely tracked the ground truth. We also systematically assessed how participation levels (app adoption and case ascertainment), technical limitations (incomplete exposure logging), and surveillance (knowledge of the background hazard from unobserved exposures) affected inference, and showed that daily population-level knowledge of the background hazard was sufficient for reliable inference. Implications of all the available evidenceBeyond their role as a control measure, DCT apps could provide timely, population-representative estimates of key transmission parameters, such as the host infectiousness profile and SI distribution. Our findings show that such inference is feasible within the privacy-preserving architectures likely to underpin future DCT systems. Greater app adoption, case ascertainment, and exposure logging would improve inference accuracy. To realise this potential, the framework will need to be embedded in DCT systems, supported by concurrent epidemiological research, real-world validation, and early collaboration with public health authorities and platform providers.

title: An integration-free CRISPR platform for genetic dissection of respiratory virus host dependencies in human nasal epithelium
abstract: Respiratory viruses, including coronaviruses, generally initiate infection in the upper respiratory tract, where mechanistic studies of host-virus interactions require models amenable to genetic manipulation. Human nasal air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures are realistic models of the nasal epithelium, but robust CRISPR/Cas9 engineering workflows for this primary cell system have been lacking. Here, we established an integration-free CRISPR/Cas9 workflow for genetic engineering of human nasal basal cells, which are subsequently differentiated into gene-edited ALI cultures. GFP-based sorting of RNP-transfected nasal basal cells substantially increases editing, achieving knockout efficiencies of 70-90% across gene targets (B2M, SLC35A1, ACE2, and TMPRSS2). Genetic disruption of ACE2 markedly reduces infection by SARS-CoV-2 and hCoV-NL63, confirming its important role for both viruses in the human nasal epithelium. TMPRSS2 knockout substantially reduces replication of both viruses, demonstrating SARS-CoV-2 depending on TMPRSS2 in the human nasal epithelium and providing genetic evidence in primary human cell cultures that hCoV-NL63 relies on TMPRSS2. This platform enables systematic genetic perturbation in a physiologically relevant model of the primary site of respiratory virus infection, validates ACE2 and TMPRSS2 as targets for medical countermeasures against SARS-CoV-2 and hCoV-NL63, and provides a versatile approach to identify host dependency factors for both circulating and emerging respiratory viruses.

title: [THE STRUCTURAL AND DYNAMIC CHARACTERISTICS OF THE DISEASES OF BLOOD CIRCULATION ORGANS IN THE KYRGYZ REPUBLIC].
abstract: The diseases of circulatory system continue to occupy leading positions in structure of morbidity and mortality of population, remaining one of key public health problems. The purpose of the study is to investigate dynamics of primary morbidity and prevalence of diseases of circulatory system by main nosological forms among adult and adolescent population of the Kyrgyz Republic in 2018-2024. The study used official data from the Center for E-Health Care that was analyzed using retrospective, statistical and comparative analytical methods. It was found that indicators of primary morbidity and prevalence were characterized by pronounced variability with greatest increase in 2022, against the background of decrease in 2020-2021, that may be due to changes in availability of medical care in period of COVID-19 pandemic. The highest levels of morbidity and prevalence were found for hypertension, coronary heart disease and cerebrovascular diseases. Some nosologies, including myocardial infarction and other peripheral vascular diseases, demonstrated sharp increase in indicators, suggesting changes in disease detection and health care seeking behavior of population. The obtained results confirm necessity to improve system of monitoring, prevention and early detection of cardiovascular diseases, especially among high-risk groups.

title: Household and Community Clustering of Concurrent Vaccine Hesitancy in China: Multicenter Survey
abstract: Abstract Background Vaccine hesitancy remains a persistent global challenge, especially in the context of major public health emergencies. While individual-level factors have been widely studied, whether and how household and community contexts shape hesitancy clustering has received little attention. Objective This study aimed to assess household- and community-level clustering of COVID-19 booster vaccine hesitancy (CBVH), identify key associated factors, and explore potential intervention targets. Methods In March 2023, a household-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults across 4 provinces. Concurrent CBVH was defined as hesitancy reported for both current and future booster intentions within the same survey. The analytical samples included 5462 participants for current CBVH, 5437 for future CBVH, and 5407 for concurrent CBVH. Three-level logistic regression models were used to quantify variance attributable to individual, household, and community levels and to identify associated factors. Network analysis was also used to examine interrelationships among key factors and identify central intervention targets. Results Among 5407 participants, 1461 (27.0%) exhibited concurrent CBVH. The unweighted prevalence of current and future CBVH was 28.4% (1553/5462) and 30.1% (1636/5437), respectively. The corresponding poststratified prevalence estimates were 30.88% and 32.55%, respectively. In the null model, the combined household- and community-level intraclass correlation coefficients were 77.73% (95% CI 72.40%‐82.29%) and 78.84% (95% CI 73.57%‐83.30%), respectively. Prior COVID-19 vaccination, self-efficacy, perceived benefits, trust in vaccine developers, and knowledge of the vaccine were associated with lower CBVH, while perceived barriers, perceived severity, household income, chronic disease, history of allergies, and living in the eastern region were associated with higher hesitancy. Network analysis revealed that self-efficacy and prior COVID-19 vaccination had the strongest associations with CBVH. Perceived barriers and trust in vaccine developers formed the strongest association among nodes. The current and future CBVH networks showed similar configurations. Conclusions The substantial household and community clustering highlights the need for group interventions. Household-centered vaccine education, community-based vaccine counseling services, and transparent vaccine communication may help reduce vaccine hesitancy and strengthen preparedness for future infectious disease outbreaks.

title: Infectious Complications in Adults Receiving Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Nosocomial and Bloodstream Infection, Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Clinical Outcomes
abstract: Background/Objectives: Reported infection rates during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) vary widely, partly because case definitions are applied inconsistently. We synthesized the prevalence and prognostic association of nosocomial and bloodstream infection (BSI) acquired during adult ECMO. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched through December 2025 for observational studies of at least 10 adults on ECMO with an explicit infection definition. We classified case definitions by the criteria actually applied. We pooled crude mortality odds ratios (ORs) and patient-level BSI prevalence in studies applying laboratory-confirmed criteria, assessed risk of bias with ROBINS-I and the JBI checklist, and rated certainty with GRADE. Results: Forty-seven reports (46 cohorts; 11,573 patients) were included. Pooled BSI prevalence was 25.8% (95% CI 17.3–36.5%; 7 studies, 1193 patients), 18.2% in pre-pandemic and 39.2% in COVID-19 cohorts (post hoc). Infection was associated with higher crude odds of death (OR 1.65, 1.33–2.04; prediction interval 0.95–2.85; 24 studies), but analyses modeling infection as time-varying were inconsistent, including no association in a multistate model (adjusted hazard ratio 1.00, 0.79–1.26), and small-study effects were suggested. Certainty was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: Roughly one in four adults on ECMO developed laboratory-confirmed BSI, more often in COVID-19 cohorts. Whether infection acquired on ECMO increases mortality remains uncertain.

title: Mortality Baselines and Excess Mortality Events in Belgian and Greek Cities Using Singular Spectrum Analysis
abstract: Background: Excess mortality estimates depend on an expected baseline, an unobservable quantity typically derived from models with prescribed functional forms and short reference periods that exclude exceptional events. Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) offers a nonparametric alternative but requires subjective component selection and is sensitive to outliers. We combined SSA with automated component selection and outlier interpolation to estimate long-term baselines and compile a catalog of excess mortality events (EMEs). Methods: We analyzed weekly all-cause mortality (2015-2024) for six metropolitan areas with contrasting climatic, demographic, and epidemiological contexts: Brussels, Antwerp, and Liege (Belgium), and Athens, Thessaloniki, and Larisa (Greece). SSA was applied to standardized log-mortality rates; components were selected using Monte Carlo SSA, and COVID-19 periods were interpolated iteratively. EMEs were defined as weeks exceeding a quasi-Poisson two-z-score threshold, then screened for coincidence with heat waves, cold waves, COVID-19 periods, and influenza epidemics. Results: Baselines were consistent within countries: annual cycles in Belgium, with an additional significant semiannual cycle in Greece reflecting summer mortality. We cataloged 170 EMEs spanning 456 weeks and 14,210 excess deaths. Pandemic weeks accounted for 77% of excess mortality, and 96 weeks coincided with temperature extremes; 56 EMEs, representing 3.7% of excess mortality, remained unmatched. Conclusions: SSA yields reproducible, low-assumption baselines that capture country-specific seasonality. Because flexible baselines can absorb recurrent seasonal mortality, component selection is a substantive choice that should be reported explicitly, together with its sensitivity.

title: [THE TRENDS OF DEVELOPMENT OF SYSTEM OF PROTECTION OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH OF GIRLS-ADOLESCENTS OF ST. PETERSBURG].
abstract: The article presents results of comprehensive analysis of gynecological morbidity of girls-adolescents 15-17 years old in St. Petersburg in 2019-2024. It is established, on the basis of preventive examinations data, that average level of pathological affect made up to 105.04‰ and had pronounced trend to decreasing (β=-4.07; p=0.048). The comparative historical analysis demonstrated improvement of reproductive health indicators by 1.9 times as compared to basic data for 1996-1997. The characteristic of structure of gynecological morbidity of modern girls-adolescents in megalopolis is predominance of menstrual disorders (90.7% of newly diagnosed cases). At that, low medical activity of girls-adolescents continues that is proved by high percentage of newly diagnosed diseases detected only during preventive examinations (29.0%) and as well as significant prevalence of general morbidity over primary one. It is established that in St. Petersburg indicators of morbidity are 2.3-2.6 times higher than the National average indicators that is related to better accessibility of medical care and more efficient system of preventive examinations in the megalopolis. The analysis of the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on gynecological morbidity of girls-adolescents revealed significant decreasing of appealability in 2020 and subsequent incomplete reestablishment of indicators that testifies structural changes in pattern of medical activity of girls-adolescents. The study confirms efficiency of the system of protection of reproductive health of girls-adolescents in St. Petersburg but at the same time indicates at necessity to further enhance medical activity of girls-adolescents and to develop target preventive programs.

title: [THE MODERN DEMOGRAPHIC CHANGES IN THE KYRGYZ REPUBLIC].
abstract: The article presents results of analysis of medical demographic indicators of the Kyrgyz Republic in 2016-2024. The study was carried out concerning dynamics of population size, natality, mortality and migration processes based on statistical data from the National Statistical Committee and the Center of E-Health Care. The regional differences in demographic trends were revealed. The high natality is specific for Southern regions, while in Northern regions its steady decreasing was fixed. It is established that COVID-19 pandemic had short-term impact on mortality growth in 2020. Despite positive natural increase, its pace is decreasing that requires elaboration of state demographic policy and mechanisms stimulating natality, population health promotion and development of regional health care infrastructure. In 2022-2023 migration flows demonstrated positive balance that reflects changes in social economic priorities of population. The main motives for migration remain low wages, limited career opportunities and uncertainty about future. The obtained results confirm necessity of systematic approach to prognostication of demographic processes and development of measures stabilizing medical demographic situation in the Republic.

title: Nosocomial Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the Post-Pandemic Era: Evolving Epidemiology and Integrated Prevention Strategies
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pandemic non-pharmaceutical interventions virtually eliminated respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) circulation in 2020–2021, and their relaxation was followed by unprecedented off-season resurgences. This narrative review, informed by a structured literature search, synthesizes current evidence on healthcare-associated RSV (HA-RSV), including transmission dynamics, vulnerable inpatient populations, and integrated prevention strategies, in the post-pandemic era. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC (January 2000–October 2025) using two complementary strategies, supplemented by WHO and CDC guidance. Primary hospital-based studies reporting laboratory-confirmed HA-RSV cases formed the core evidence set; surveillance reports, systematic reviews, and guidance were used as labeled contextual evidence and synthesized narratively. Results: Twenty-nine primary studies from neonatal, pediatric, adult, geriatric, and immunocompromised settings provided direct evidence on HA-RSV, which accounted for 3–15% of RSV hospitalizations depending on setting and case definition and was associated with prolonged stay, escalation of respiratory support, higher costs, and, in children, higher mortality than community-onset infection. Universal masking and pre-admission screening were followed by reductions in HA-RSV in most before–after studies. Post-pandemic surveillance shows earlier, less predictable RSV activity and periods of concurrent circulation with influenza and SARS-CoV-2. RSV spreads mainly through short-range respiratory particles and contaminated hands and surfaces; asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic healthcare workers are one potential source of introduction. Conclusions: Prevention of HA-RSV rests on hand hygiene, transmission-based precautions, environmental disinfection, rapid molecular diagnostics, and supportive healthcare-worker and visitor policies, escalated according to local surveillance rather than the calendar. Immunoprophylaxis and vaccination reduce severe RSV disease in eligible groups, but direct evidence that they prevent healthcare-associated transmission is lacking.

title: Vaccinations in pregnancy: An update for a changing time.
abstract: Maternal immunization is one of the most effective public health interventions to reduce infectious morbidity and mortality in pregnant women, fetuses, and newborns. Despite robust evidence supporting vaccine safety and effectiveness in pregnancy, global uptake has declined following the COVID-19 pandemic, contributing to resurgent outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases. While national immunization schedules vary, there is broad international consensus recommending influenza and tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccination during pregnancy, with increasing adoption of maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunization. This review provides an updated, globally relevant summary of recommended vaccines before, during, and after pregnancy, highlights vaccines under development, and discusses implementation challenges. Strengthening maternal immunization requires coordinated action across governments, healthcare systems, industry, and media to improve access, trust, and equity in vaccine delivery.

title: Epidemiology of foodborne pathogens in Europe with special emphasis on the Republic of Croatia
abstract: This review evaluates the occurrence and epidemiological trends of major foodborne zoonotic pathogens in the European Union, with particular emphasis on the Republic of Croatia, over the period 2020-2024. Using the One Health framework, data were synthesised from annual zoonosis reports of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), complemented by targeted national and regional studies. Following a temporary, pandemic-related decline in 2020, largely attributable to COVID-19 related disruptions in surveillance and behavioral changes, notification rates for most foodborne pathogens rebounded and stabilised at pre-pandemic or higher levels. Campylobacteriosis remained the most frequently reported zoonosis, while salmonellosis persisted at consistently high levels, with notable shifts in serovar distribution, including the emergence of Salmonella Infantis. Listeriosis, although less frequent, demonstrated the highest hospitalisation and case fatality rates, with a continued upward trend. Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections increased substantially, partly due to improved molecular diagnostics and enhanced surveillance sensitivity. Unlike existing consolidated EFSA/ECDC reports, this review highlights the importance of regional data for identifying localised hotspots and more precisely understanding transmission dynamics. This more detailed perspective emphasises the need for continuous, integrated surveillance across the human, veterinary, and environmental sectors to effectively address evolving, region-specific risks related to pathogen adaptation, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-related pressures within the food supply chain.

title: Achieving near single-molecule sensitivity in separation-free protein detection using engineered kinetic proofreading
abstract: Unlike nucleic acids, proteins cannot be directly amplified. Ultrasensitive detection must therefore couple efficient analyte-to-signal conversion with strong suppression of target-independent background. Consistently detecting ~100 molecules (below which Poisson sampling noise alone causes CV to exceed 10%) across protein targets in a format as scalable and accessible as PCR remains unsolved. Separation-based ultrasensitive immunoassays require target binding stable enough to survive stringent washing and are therefore constrained by wash-induced signal loss and, more fundamentally, the relative scarcity of exceptionally tight binders. Performance consequently varies across targets; detection limits below 1,000 molecules remain rare. Conventional separation-free proximity assays avoid washing but incur background from random probe collisions, with reported detection limits frequently exceeding 100,000 molecules. Here we introduce Successive Proximity Extension Amplification Reaction (SPEAR), a separation-free architecture in which autonomous engineered DNA nanodevices emulate biological kinetic proofreading. Two successive irreversible proximity-extension steps compound discrimination between analyte-dependent and background reactions, suppressing spurious signals while preserving efficient analyte-to-signal conversion. This design reduces reliance on high-affinity binders and enables sub-fM detection from 1 uL samples through simple 3-step mixing followed by standard qPCR readout. Across 11 biomarkers tested, SPEAR consistently achieved sub-100-molecule detection limits. Where compared, it outperformed ultrasensitive separation-based platforms, analytically and clinically, including for low-abundance Alzheimer's disease biomarkers. SPEAR also precisely quantified SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody titers from finger-prick dried blood spots, concordant with the cell-based reference assay on venous blood. It detected a distinct mixed phosphorylation state of Tau, and targeting this state resolved previously observed capillary-venous discordance and improved amyloid-status discrimination. These results establish engineered autonomous successive molecular discrimination as a practical strategy for near-single-molecule protein detection, extending the sensitivity, scalability and accessibility of PCR-based testing to non-amplifiable analytes.

title: Adrenal Infections: An Underrecognized Cause of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency.
abstract: INTRODUCTION Adrenal infections are an underrecognized but clinically significant cause of primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI). OBJECTIVES This review proposes a diagnostic algorithm for the evaluation of suspected cases. RESULTS The most common causative pathogens are Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Histoplasma capsulatum; however, bacterial infections and viral pathogens such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) have also been reported. These infections, particularly in tuberculosis and histoplasmosis, can induce granulomatous inflammation, tissue necrosis, and destruction of the adrenal glands, leading to systemic symptoms and hormonal deficiency. The prevalence of adrenal insufficiency varies widely, ranging from 14% to 100%, depending on the study population and diagnostic criteria. Affected patients may present across a broad clinical spectrum, from chronic adrenal insufficiency to adrenal crisis, and some patients may be identified incidentally through imaging performed for unrelated indications. Computed tomography is the primary imaging modality for diagnosing adrenal infection, typically demonstrating bilateral adrenal lesions characterized by hypodensity with central necrosis, peripheral rim enhancement, and calcification. In contrast, during the late phase, the adrenal glands progressively decrease in size and may become atrophic, particularly in tuberculosis, and often with persistent calcifications. Tissue biopsy with histopathological examination and culture remains the definitive diagnostic tool to confirm the infectious etiology. CONCLUSIONS Early recognition is essential, as management requires two complementary approaches: 1. antimicrobial therapy directed at the causative pathogen, and 2. hormonal replacement in patients with established adrenal insufficiency and longitudinal hormonal surveillance in those with preserved adrenal reserve at initial presentation.

title: Macroeconomic and Global Financial Determinants of NIFTY 50 Volatility in India: Evidence from Monetary Policy, Exchange Rate, Capital Flows and Global Uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Background Indian equity-market volatility is increasingly influenced by the interaction between domestic macroeconomic conditions and global financial developments. Changes in monetary policy, exchange rates, foreign portfolio investment and global uncertainty may affect investor expectations and financial-market stability, but their relative importance can vary across economic regimes. Objective This study examines the macroeconomic and global financial determinants of NIFTY 50 volatility in India, with particular emphasis on how these relationships evolve across major domestic and international economic episodes. Methods Using high-frequency NIFTY 50 market data and corresponding macro-financial indicators for 2015–2026 , the study investigates the relationship between NIFTY 50 volatility and monetary-policy conditions, INR/USD exchange-rate movements, foreign portfolio investment flows and global financial uncertainty. The analysis distinguishes four periods: 2015–2019 (pre-COVID), 2020–2021 (COVID-19 shock and recovery), 2022–2023 (global monetary tightening), and 2024–2026 (evolving geopolitical, trade and financial environment) . NIFTY 50 returns and conditional volatility are modelled using ARCH/GARCH-family specifications, including asymmetric volatility models, diagnostic tests and regime-based robustness analysis. Results The empirical framework evaluates whether domestic monetary conditions, exchange-rate movements, capital-flow dynamics and global uncertainty are significantly associated with NIFTY 50 volatility and whether the magnitude of these relationships differs across the four identified periods. The study reports model estimates, diagnostic statistics and robustness results to assess the stability of the observed relationships across changing macro-financial conditions. Conclusions The study provides an integrated empirical assessment of the domestic and global determinants of Indian equity-market volatility over a period encompassing pre-pandemic conditions, the COVID-19 shock and recovery, global monetary tightening, and the subsequent geopolitical and trade environment. The findings are intended to contribute to the understanding of financial-market volatility in an emerging economy and provide evidence relevant to financial-stability monitoring, monetary-policy assessment and international capital-market risk management.

title: Vaccination perspectives among nurses in a rural, frontier state.
abstract: BACKGROUND During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, the nursing profession, particularly in rural and frontier states, faced substantial challenges due to vaccine hesitancy. Higher hesitancy among nurses compared to other health professionals may have contributed to elevated infection and death rates in one rural, frontier state. PURPOSE This study investigated vaccine-related attitudes, beliefs, and perceptions among practicing nurses, faculty, and students in a state heavily affected by the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. title: Hospital Mortality Considering Comorbidity and Patient Age Across Successive Epidemic Waves: A Descriptive Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Comorbidity increases the risk of adverse outcomes in COVID-19; therefore, a systematic assessment of the pattern of concomitant diseases and the demographic characteristics of deceased patients is necessary for subsequent risk stratification and justifying patient triage in a hospital setting. AIM: To analyze the association of comorbid pathology with in-hospital mortality in patients with COVID-19 based on the assessment of the pattern of concomitant diseases and the age of patients who died in the hospital. METHODS: A descriptive study (case series) of in-hospital deaths among patients with COVID-19 was conducted at the Republican Clinical Hospital named after Prof. Agafonov, Ministry of Health of the Republic of Tatarstan, in 2020–2022. Deaths among patients aged ≥18 years with confirmed COVID-19 were included if the minimally necessary data were available: age, sex, year of death, and concomitant diagnoses coded in accordance with the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision. Age- and sex-related characteristics, the distribution of deaths by year, and the frequency of concomitant conditions coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (0, absence; 1, presence) were assessed, with acute complications analyzed separately. Descriptive statistics were used (median [Me], interquartile range [Q1–Q3], proportions with 95% CIs), as well as between-group comparisons (χ2 or Fisher exact test), with p 0.05 considered statistically significant. RESULTS: The maximum proportion of deaths was registered among patients aged 60–74 years (42.6%), which allows this group to be considered the “core” of in-hospital mortality. Among the deceased, women predominated (62.3%), and their proportion increased in older groups (p = 5.22 × 10−5). The temporal structure of deaths was characterized by their concentration in 2021 (84.3%) compared with 2020 (10.4%) and 2022 (5.3%). The comorbidity profile was predominantly represented by chronic non-infectious diseases: arterial hypertension (81.7%), chronic heart failure (58.4%), chronic ischemic heart disease (33.1%), conduction disorders (12.3%), and atrial fibrillation/flutter (11.7%); type 2 diabetes mellitus (35.9%), obesity (29.0%), chronic kidney disease (20.4%), and anemia (17.5%). CONCLUSION: In-hospital mortality in COVID-19 was predominantly formed among older patients with severe comorbidity; age and sex must be taken into account in subsequent multifactorial models and in the development of recommendations for risk stratification and patient triage.

title: Knowledge, trust, and multidimensional perceptions of human papillomavirus vaccination among women attending a single primary care centre in Astana, Kazakhstan: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Kazakhstan reintroduced human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination in 2024, making public confidence and communication important. This study described HPV knowledge and trust in information sources and exploratorily examined vaccine-perception structure and correlates among women attending primary care in Astana. A cross-sectional electronic survey was conducted from 17 January to 28 February 2026 among 221 adult women recruited through convenience sampling. HPV knowledge, source-specific trust, and 16 perception items were assessed. Exploratory psychometric analysis used polychoric correlations, parallel analysis, and principal-axis factor analysis with oblimin rotation to derive preliminary composite measures. Spearman correlations and robust multivariable linear models examined safety concern and perceived effectiveness. A secondary logistic model examined refusal or intention to refuse HPV vaccination for a daughter. Mean HPV knowledge was 4.95 ± 3.84 of 12. A five-item safety concern measure (mean 2.34 ± 0.97; α = 0.868; ω = 0.901) and a three-item perceived effectiveness measure (mean 3.20 ± 1.24; α = 0.922; ω = 0.948) were derived. Knowledge correlated negatively with safety concern ( ρ = −0.284, p < 0.001) and positively with perceived effectiveness ( ρ = 0.393, p < 0.001). Safety concern was associated with COVID-19 controversy spillover (B = 0.190, 95% CI 0.043−0.337), earlier-programme distrust (B = 0.197, 95% CI 0.047−0.347), and preference for natural immunity (B = 0.137, 95% CI 0.040−0.234). Higher knowledge (B = 0.061, 95% CI 0.010−0.111) and professional/scientific trust (B = 0.297, 95% CI 0.114−0.480) were associated with greater perceived effectiveness. Forty-nine participants (22.2%) reported refusal or intention to refuse vaccination for a daughter; knowing someone believed to have become seriously ill after vaccination was associated with this response (aOR 7.42, 95% CI 2.60−21.16). HPV vaccine perceptions were multidimensional. Knowledge and professional-scientific trust were linked mainly to perceived effectiveness, whereas safety concerns were more strongly related to vaccine narratives. Communication strategies should combine factual education with transparent safety dialogue and clinician communication.

title: Mapping policy architecture for vaccine research, development and manufacturing in Africa: a scoping review protocol
abstract: Introduction: Despite the unprecedented speed of COVID-19 vaccine development, manufacturing capacity remained geographically concentrated in high-income and some emerging economies and was insufficient to meet global demand promptly and equitably. This constrained production capacity, together with domestic political pressures and market power asymmetries, contributed to vaccine nationalism. Therefore, to secure Africa’s future access to vaccines, the African Union aims to produce at least 60 percent of the vaccines consumed locally in Africa by 2040, up from less than one percent, as part of the broader health security and future pandemic response agenda. Achieving this vision requires proactive policy coherence and coordination across the continent to prevent duplication of efforts, waste and unhealthy competition. Consequently, this review aims to map, assess and compare the content of national, regional, and continental-level policies for vaccine R&D and manufacturing in Africa, generating actionable insights to inform coordinated strategies and advance the AU’s 2040 vaccine manufacturing goal. Methods and analysis The review will be conducted following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute’s methodological guidance for scoping reviews. Reporting will adhere to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Policy instruments relevant to human vaccine R&D and manufacturing in Africa will be included as the primary unit of analysis. The sources of evidence are policy databases – Overton, Policy Commons, and ProQuest Policy File Index – and the official websites of relevant governments, regional and continental institutions. The search will focus on Africa, using key terms relating to vaccine policies. Two independent reviewers will screen the retrieved documents in Covidence, and data extraction will be conducted using a pretested template in Microsoft Excel 2021. This review does not require ethical approval. Conclusion The results will contribute to the academic literature on vaccine security and the policy architecture for vaccine R&D and manufacturing in Africa.

title: Acute Stress Orthomolecular Nutrition (ASON): A Systems-Medicine Hypothesis and Framework for Dynamic Nutrient Requirements
abstract: Acute stress can change metabolism, immune activity, redox regulation, microcirculation, nutrient distribution, tissue repair, and the interaction among these systems. These changes raise the possibility that the functional availability or requirement for selected nutrients differs temporarily from that during physiological maintenance. Acute Stress Orthomolecular Nutrition (ASON) is proposed as a systems-medicine hypothesis and research framework for investigating this possibility across infection, including COVID-19; surgery, including dental procedures; trauma and burns; ischemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular injury; intense physical exertion and recovery; and, more provisionally, acute neuroendocrine or psychological stress.The framework distinguishes altered circulating concentration, altered turnover or loss, functional nutrient limitation, and clinical benefit from intervention. None establishes the next automatically. ASON further treats nutrient physiology as one component of a changing biological terrain in which metabolic state, inflammatory burden, redox signaling, microcirculation, organ function, baseline nutritional status, environmental exposures, and repair capacity may interact. Selected perioperative nutritional strategies provide clinical precedents, but uncertainty in systematic reviews and null or harmful results in critical illness impose substantial boundaries. ASON neither predicts uniformly increased requirements nor supports universal high-dose supplementation. Nutrient effects must be evaluated according to baseline status, stressor, disease severity, organ function, formulation, dose, route, timing, and duration.This narrative framework proposes serial systems-level physiological measurements followed by prespecified, adequately controlled intervention studies with patient-centered outcomes and adverse-event monitoring. Its incremental value would depend on demonstrating reproducible stress-related changes, identifying functionally relevant limitations, and, separately, showing that targeted interventions improve outcomes safely. Acute psychological stress remains a hypothesis-generating extension without an established acute nutrient-treatment indication.

title: Mapping programmable mRNA research relevant to cancer-associated immune escape: a dual-database bibliometric and topic modeling analysis
abstract: Programmable messenger RNA (mRNA) platforms can encode tumor antigens or immunomodulators, enabling coordinated antigen delivery and immune modulation. Yet the literature spans cancer vaccination, delivery engineering, immune biology, and adjacent infectious-disease research, making its structure and evidentiary boundaries difficult to discern. We mapped this cross-domain corpus to clarify its development, organization, and relevance to cancer-associated immune escape. We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus on July 29, 2026, for English-language Articles and Reviews published since 2006. The strategy combined programmable or therapeutic mRNA, cancer, and immune-escape-related concepts. R-based analyses summarized the number of publications (NP), total citations (TC), and collaboration patterns; BERTopic modeled titles and abstracts after entity-aware preprocessing. Independent two-author review supported the five topic labels and characterized the outliers, and robustness was assessed across alternative clustering configurations. The dataset comprised 756 publications (NP = 756). Annual output increased more than fourfold in 2021 and reached NP = 182 in 2025. China (NP = 291; 38.49%) and the United States (NP = 146; 19.31%) accounted for nearly 58% of corresponding-author publications. Sichuan University and Frontiers in Immunology ranked first in institutional and journal output, respectively. Nature had the highest retained source-record citation total (TC = 2,326). BERTopic assigned 745 publications to five topics, while 11 of 756 records remained outliers (1.46%). The topics represented mRNA delivery and immunomodulatory cancer-vaccine research (52.1%), SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in oncology and immunotherapy settings (23.6%), therapeutic mRNA cancer-vaccine platforms (13.3%), tumor-antigen discovery and immune-subtype stratification (8.6%), and mRNA-vaccine immunogenicity during autoimmune immunosuppression (2.4%). Publication activity in the retrieved cross-domain corpus expanded rapidly after 2020. The corpus included both direct cancer-mRNA research and adjacent platform or immune-response literature. By distinguishing these components and identifying thematic connections among delivery, antigen selection, immune context, and collaboration, the analysis provides an evidence-navigation framework for prioritizing systematic reviews, mechanistic studies, and clinical evaluation. The map does not itself establish therapeutic efficacy.

title: Balancing Burden and Agency: African States’ Diplomatic Strategies in Global Health Governance
abstract: Abstract Background African states bear a disproportionate share of the global disease burden, yet they have historically occupied the margins of agenda-setting in global health governance, where dependency and developmentalist framings cast them as recipients of aid rather than authors of policy. This article asks how African states assert agency and influence within global health governance despite, and at times through, that structural burden. It advances a framework of ‘agency under constraint’ and specifies observable mechanisms through which structurally weak actors widen their room for manoeuvring. Methods This study employs a qualitative, documentary design focusing on bounded diplomatic episodes spanning from the COVID-19 pandemic to early 2026. Using a purposively selected sample, the research conducts a structured thematic comparison of primary official texts, institutional communiqués, negotiation records, vetted news reports, and peer-reviewed scholarship. The episodes are analyzed to trace diplomatic practice, negotiating posture, and institutional engagement, evaluating how strategies shift across different governance arenas Results The analysis identifies two complementary diplomatic strategies employed by African states. First, in multilateral arenas, states utilize collective action through regional integration to pool sovereignty and amplify bargaining weight. This is evidenced by the autonomous elevation of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, pooled vaccine procurement platforms, the African Medicines Agency, and coalition diplomacy regarding intellectual property waivers. Second, in bilateral arenas, states deploy strategic "(de)partnership" to manage dominant patrons. This involves resisting asymmetrical terms in health agreements, such as mandatory epidemiological data-sharing without guaranteed benefit-sharing, while diversifying partnerships to mitigate risk. However, this agency remains structurally bounded. Collective efforts occasionally face material vetoes from resource-rich states, and diversifying partners may merely substitute one form of dependency for another. Conclusions For structurally constrained actors, diplomatic agency is better defined as the strategic management of a portfolio of dependencies rather than the absolute attainment of autonomy. By outlining how and when structural burden is converted into leverage, this research contributes to debates on African agency and underscores the necessity of treating African institutions as vital co-architects of global health governance.

title: Trends in Healthcare-Associated Infections and Antimicrobial Use in a Paediatric Hospital from Bucharest, Romania, Across the Pre-Pandemic, Pandemic, and Post-Pandemic Periods (2017–2024)
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic and the broader epidemiological context may have affected healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and antimicrobial use (AU), including among the paediatric population. This study used seven point prevalence surveys (PPSs) to characterise HAIs and AU and to observe trends over time at a paediatric hospital in Bucharest. We collected data from 977 patients and identified 31 HAIs in 28 patients with an overall prevalence of 2.9%. During the COVID-19 years, prevalence was higher (4.0%), but no trend was detected. AU prevalence was 72.6%, with no specific trend across the study period (p = 0.48) overall or by ward. Most prescribed antibiotics were from the Watch category (65.5%), with an upward trend across the study period (p < 0.0001), while the Access category registered a downward trend. In conclusion, HAI prevalence did not vary significantly with the epidemiological context. Antibiotic use in the Watch category increased during the pandemic, while the Access category declined. These findings highlight the importance of surveillance for infection prevention and control at the hospital level, and the need for antimicrobial stewardship, guidelines, and continuing medical education on appropriate prescribing practices in paediatric care.

We collected data from 977 patients and identified 31 HAIs in 28 patients with an overall prevalence of 2.9%. During the COVID-19 years, prevalence was higher (4.0%), but no trend was detected. AU prevalence was 72.6%, with no specific trend across the study period (p = 0.48) overall or by ward. Most prescribed antibiotics were from the Watch category (65.5%), with an upward trend across the study period (p < 0.0001), while the Access category registered a downward trend. In conclusion, HAI prevalence did not vary significantly with the epidemiological context. Antibiotic use in the Watch category increased during the pandemic, while the Access category declined. These findings highlight the importance of surveillance for infection prevention and control at the hospital level, and the need for antimicrobial stewardship, guidelines, and continuing medical education on appropriate prescribing practices in paediatric care.

title: Independent Agencies, Regulation‐Compliant Citizens? Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Vaccine Authorization in the EU
abstract: The effectiveness of regulatory policy in many areas is contingent on citizens adhering to the scientific advice of regulatory bodies. This in turn depends on whether they perceive this advice as credible . One of the biggest threats to regulatory credibility is the concern that regulatory policy can be tainted by short‐term political interests. Consequently, regulation literature points to agency independence as a crucial resource to securing regulatory credibility, which in turn fosters citizen compliance. We test this assumption both observationally and experimentally in the case of the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) risk assessment for the first COVID‐19 vaccine—a prime example of reliance on credibility in regulation under conditions of controversy and concerns over political interference. We conducted a pre‐registered survey experiment with 4000 EU citizens from four countries timed shortly after the vaccine's approval and before its mass distribution. The results provide partial support that independence is beneficial to regulatory credibility and by extension, to regulatory compliance. Citizens who perceive the EMA as more independent found its risk assessment to be more credible and were more willing to take the vaccine. However, our experimental evidence is less conclusive. Thus, while independence might not in and of itself be a “silver bullet” to ensure regulatory credibility and compliance, it does play an important role, and its real‐life substantive significance would scale up considerably at population levels.

title: Appropriateness of respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms: A retrospective observational study.
abstract: BACKGROUND Respiratory viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV place considerable pressure on healthcare systems. Inconsistent respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms may delay recognition of respiratory viral infections and implementation of appropriate infection prevention and control measures. OBJECTIVE To assess the appropriateness of respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms and to identify factors associated with inappropriate screening. METHODS We conducted a retrospective observational study in a 2500-bed tertiary hospital in Belgium during three periods of the 2022-2023 influenza epidemic. Medical records were reviewed for demographic and clinical characteristics, respiratory symptoms, and respiratory virus screening practices. Screening was classified as appropriate or inappropriate (delayed or absent despite indication) based on prevailing guidelines. Determinants of inappropriate screening were explored using univariable analyses. RESULTS Of 743 hospital admissions assessed for eligibility, 345 (46%) involved patients with respiratory symptoms and constituted the primary analysis population. Respiratory virus screening was appropriate in 75% (258/345) and inappropriate in 25% (87/345) of cases. Appropriate screening was more frequent among patients admitted for respiratory conditions and among those meeting criteria for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI). Screening appropriateness was significantly lower among patients who developed respiratory symptoms during hospitalization than among those with symptoms documented at admission (37% vs. Isolation status could not be reliably determined for 44% of patients and was therefore considered descriptive only. CONCLUSION Gaps remain in appropriate respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms, particularly among patients who develop symptoms during hospitalization. Systematic symptom-based screening and standardized decision-support tools may help improve adherence to respiratory virus screening recommendations.

title: Prospective cohort study for digital health research in Germany (DigiHero): objectives, design and baseline characteristics
abstract: DigiHero is a population based, nationwide digital cohort study with participants from more than 120 000 households from all federal states in Germany. It was set up during the COVID-19 pandemic to contribute to the rapid collection of COVID-19 related data but already at its set-up, it was intended to be a research platform to study (chronic) diseases, health behaviour, and healthy ageing. Later on, it became part of the German Center for Mental Health and contributes to its research agenda. Participants were recruited via postal invitations with address information obtained from administrative registries; the participation is fully online, with four regular contacts per year. A wide array of exposures is being assessed, with particular focus on change over time. In addition to regularly repeated modules, the flexibility of the study design allows to implement further questionnaires responding to newly emerging health topics. Self-collected bio samples or examinations in study centers or even in medical practices can be included in subprojects. Data from wearables, sensors, and linked health insurance data will enrich the responses to questionnaires. With focus on new digital approaches, DigiHero can react directly and quickly to current health issues, generating health-related data promptly and cost-effectively. Given its fully virtual participation, DigiHero supplements local or study-center associated cohorts in Germany. It is intended to reflect regional heterogeneity with inclusion of rural regions across Germany.

title: Methodological landscapes in tourism crisis management: A systematic mapping review of research designs, 2007–2025
abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThis study systematically reviews methodological approaches in tourism crisis management research, examining 374 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus and published between 2007 and 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, 411 records were identified through a structured Scopus search, and 37 were excluded during screening (15 not substantively addressing crisis management in tourism and 22 falling outside the 2007–2025 window), yielding a final sample of 374 articles. Each article was classified along two dimensions: crisis type (COVID-19/health, war/political/terrorism, natural disaster, financial/economic, or general) and research methodology (paradigm, specific methods, analytical techniques). Classification drew on titles, abstracts, and author keywords rather than full texts; findings should be interpreted accordingly. Because the search string required at least one methodology-related term, the corpus represents the methodology-signaling segment of the literature, and reported shares should be read within that scope. The findings reveal a corpus dominated by qualitative research (56.4% of articles), led by interviews (34.2%) and surveys (21.7%). COVID-19 and health-related crises account for 57.2% of the corpus, confirming a strong post-2020 concentration. Experimental designs appear in 0.8% of articles and longitudinal designs in 2.7%. In comparison, mixed methods research remains at 5.9%, indicating persistent gaps in designs best suited to causal inference and to tracking crises over time. The study contributes a five-category crisis typology, an evidence-based diagnostic of methodological strengths and gaps, and a research agenda for methodological diversification. Practically, stronger and more diverse methodologies improve the evidence base for tourism organizations, destination authorities, and public administrators making decisions under uncertainty.

title: The Perception of Quality of Care and Respect of Human Rights in Mental Health Facilities Among Health Workers Over Time in Sardinia, Italy.
abstract: OBJECTIVES To examine changes in mental health workers' (MHWs) perceptions of human rights protection and job satisfaction before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy (Sardinia). STUDY DESIGN Comparative analysis of three cross-sectional surveys conducted at different time points. METHODS Three cross-sectional surveys were carried out among MHWs working in community mental health services in Italy (Sardinia) in 2019 (pre-COVID), 2022 (during COVID), and 2025 (post-COVID). Participants completed the Well-Being at Work and Respect for Human Rights Questionnaire (WWRR). Items 1 to 6 (Likert scale 1-6) assessed job satisfaction and perceived respect for human rights, while item 7 evaluated perceived staff shortages. Comparisons across surveys were performed using ANOVA and χ2 tests. RESULTS The samples included 126 MHWs in 2019, 240 in 2022, and 101 in 2025. The proportion of older staff increased significantly over time (p < .001). Satisfaction with work and organizational aspects improved across the three periods, along with perceptions of respect for users' and staff human rights. Satisfaction with available resources peaked in 2022 and declined in the post-pandemic period. The perceived need for psychologists and rehabilitation professionals remained consistently high, while the perceived shortage of nurses and physicians decreased over time. CONCLUSIONS Perceived respect for human rights and job satisfaction among MHWs showed a sustained improvement after the COVID-19 pandemic, supporting the resilience of Italy's community psychiatry model. Ongoing concerns regarding resources underscore the need for renewed investment in human capital.

title: Field or virtual? Perceived impact of academic excursions through the eyes of (future) hydrologists
abstract: Field training such as excursions has always been an integral part of the education of geoscientists. The value of these excursions is frequently debated, related to the efforts and costs involved with their organization. Professionally prepared virtual excursions are sometimes presented as a possible alternative for field activities. This debate has been accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic: the lockdown forced teachers to come up with virtual and online educational material, also for fieldwork and excursions. One of the courses at Wageningen University (the Netherlands) that was heavily affected by COVID-19 restrictions was the Master course Catchment and Climate Hydrology. An important and integral component of that course is an 8 d excursion to Iceland where relatively undisturbed catchments are studied in a country heavily affected by climate change. All students from the 2020 and 2021 cohort took the alternative professionally prepared virtual excursion. After the pandemic, in 2022, these students were offered to join an extra added excursion. About 50 % of that population was able to join. This configuration, involving student cohorts that participated only in the field excursion, only in the virtual excursion, or in both, provided an unique opportunity to assess student evaluations of field-based education and the potential of virtual alternatives. A questionnaire was sent to excursion participants to critically evaluate the impact of the excursion on their scientific development and their view on real versus virtual excursions for geoscientists. The time frame for the questionnaire ran from 2011 to 2025, including COVID-19 years 2020 and 2021. The response on the statement “Planning and/or fieldwork are an important part of my current job or study” is moderately agree , with > 50 % of the responses even with a response strongly to fully agree. This indicates that field training is very important for the majority of the junior and senior geoscientists. The study also showed that a multiple day excursion to Iceland strongly contributed to the understanding of undisturbed hydrologic systems and to the general scientific development of the participants. The survey clearly indicated that they appreciated the effort of making a virtual excursion, but that the impact of that virtual excursion on their scientific development was considerably lower than for the equivalent real excursion. The reasons indicated are manifold: they missed the active location-based learning in a country with undisturbed catchments, the inspirational and direct interaction with the teaching staff and linking up with their peers to create a professional network. Therefor the main conclusion of this inventory is that preparing virtual excursions for Master students can be worth the investment, but just as an extra tool in the course tool box, and certainly not as a replacement for real excursions.

title: Clinical validation of a novel multiplex real-time PCR for diagnosing community-acquired pneumonia in the emergency department: a promising diagnostic tool for Mycoplasma pneumoniae
abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a global public health burden with high morbidity, but timely diagnosis is hindered by limitations of conventional methods. We validated a novel multiplex real-time PCR (mRT-PCR) for CAP diagnosis in the emergency department, focusing on Mycoplasma pneumoniae ( M. A retrospective cohort of 371 CAP patients (2019–2021) from the Chinese PLA General Hospital was enrolled. The panel targeted 85 pathogens (40 bacteria, 18 viruses, 17 fungi, 10 other) plus 8 resistance genes, with a turnaround time (TAT) under 4 h and a cost of approximately US$100 per test. mRT-PCR showed performance comparable to mNGS for common pathogens (concordance >69% for bacteria/fungi) and high concordance with the final clinical diagnosis. Notably, it detected M. pneumoniae in 36.7% (136/371) of cases, outperforming conventional methods by identifying 204 exclusive positives (55.0% of cohort), with M. pneumoniae (40%) and viruses (30%) predominating. Polymicrobial infections occurred in 36.1% of cases; M. pneumoniae co-infections (38 cases) showed elevated neutrophils and reduced lymphocytes vs. An independent reference standard analysis excluding both index tests showed that 24.1% (210/873) of calls were independently corroborated - high for influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and M. pneumoniae , lower for S. pneumoniae , consistent with the limited sensitivity of sputum culture. Unlike conventional syndromic panels such as FilmArray, which profile fewer targets without concurrent resistance-gene detection, this mRT-PCR combines broad coverage with rapid TAT and low cost, making it promising for timely CAP diagnosis, particularly in resource-limited settings and for targeted therapy.

title: Lessons learned from using high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtration units in care homes: interviews with care home staff, residents and relatives from the AFRI-c trial
abstract: Background: Respiratory infections are a leading cause of mortality and morbidity among older adults in residential care homes. We conducted a qualitative study within the ‘Air Filtration to prevent symptomatic winter Respiratory Infections (including COVID-19) in care homes (AFRI-c)’ pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial. This paper reports the lessons learned from using high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtration units in a care home setting. Methods Interviews with care home staff (n=25), residents (n=20), and relatives (n=12) who participated in the AFRI-c trial were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Preventing respiratory infections was a high priority for staff. Although using HEPA filters became normalised during the intervention period, they were not considered suitable for all residents. The ability to lock settings or fix them to walls was identified as a potential way to improve them in this setting. Participants felt that the care home sector would be unable to afford the cost of HEPA filters for all residents and that their use would be prioritised for those with the greatest need. However, without financial support, HEPA filters may only be used by residents who can afford them. Staff felt that HEPA filters might be attractive to potential residents and their families, but consultees and residents were both more focused on overall quality of care and life. Maintenance of the HEPA filters had a minor impact on staff workload. Conclusions Although the AFRI-c trial found that HEPA filters did not reduce respiratory infections in residents, these insights could be valuable for care homes wishing to use HEPA filters for other reasons, such as reducing airborne pollutants and allergens. With some adaptions, portable HEPA filters could be made more suitable for use in care home settings. There were concerns that without financial support, inequalities could deepen.

With some adaptions, portable HEPA filters could be made more suitable for use in care home settings. There were concerns that without financial support, inequalities could deepen.

title: Anxiety and Depression Among Residents of the Professors' Estate, University of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background Anxiety and depressive disorders are leading causes of morbidity and disability worldwide, with a marked increase since the COVID-19 pandemic. In sub-Saharan Africa, these issues are amplified by unfavorable socio-economic conditions, limited access to mental health services, and strong stigma surrounding psychological disorders. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), studies on mental health in the university setting remain limited. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of anxiety and depressive disorders and identify associated factors among residents of the "Plateau des Professeurs" of the University of Kinshasa. Methods A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted at the “Plateau des Professeurs” estate of the University of Kinshasa, DRC, from December 2025 to January 2026. An exhaustive sampling method was used, including all eligible households. Anxiety and depressive disorders were measured using the Hopkins Symptom Checklist-25 (HSCL-25), with a threshold of ≥ 1.75 defining a probable case. Bivariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with anxio-depressive disorders. Results A total of 201 residents were included. The mean age was over 65 years for 49.3% of participants, and 74.1% were male. The prevalence of anxiety was 29.4% (95% CI: 23.4–36.1), depression 15.9% (95% CI: 11.5–21.7), and concomitant anxio-depressive disorders 19.9% (95% CI: 14.9–26.0). In multivariate analysis, administrative staff had a significantly higher risk of anxio-depressive disorders (adjusted OR 6.79, 95% CI: 2.29–20.15; p = 0.001) compared with academic staff, as did scientific staff (adjusted OR 5.13, 95% CI: 1.92–13.73; p = 0.001). Lack of supervisor support was also independently associated with anxio-depressive disorders (adjusted OR 2.81, 95% CI: 1.17–6.74; p = 0.021). Conclusions Nearly one in five residents of the University of Kinshasa Professors' Estate met criteria for probable anxio-depressive disorder. Administrative and scientific staff were disproportionately affected, and lack of supervisor support tripled the risk. These findings support the implementation of targeted mental health interventions and leadership training programs within the university setting in the DRC.

title: A Structured Decision-Support Framework for Technology Adoption to Advance Airport Sustainability and Resilience
abstract: Airports face challenges in integrating sustainability and resilience into their long-term operational plans due to climate change, regulatory mandates, financial constraints, and disruptions such as the COVID-19 pandemic. While technology adoption plays a key role in addressing these issues, many airports lack structured strategies for evaluating, selecting, and implementing sustainability and resilience-focused innovations. Technology is often adopted reactively, driven by crises or regulatory compliance, rather than through proactive, strategic planning. This study introduces an empirically supported decision-support framework that combines established technology adoption models, sustainability and resilience assessment logic, and airport-specific implementation needs into a structured process for sustainable and resilient technology adoption. The framework synthesizes engineering-based maturity assessment, strategic planning, cross-disciplinary implementation, and Envision-based sustainability and resilience criteria, providing a tool that merges engineering judgment with organizational, regulatory, and environmental considerations. It equips airport decision-makers with a practical methodology for aligning technological innovation with operational performance, sustainability objectives, and long-term adaptability. The framework was empirically supported through expert input and statistical analyses of survey responses representing 27 commercial airports across the United States. An illustrative case study demonstrates an application of the framework by translating strategic sustainability and resilience goals into actionable implementation steps. This study contributes to the body of knowledge by presenting an evidence-based decision-support methodology that bridges the gap among strategic commitments and implementation, supports decarbonization, operational resilience, and infrastructure sustainability, while providing practical guidance for planners, sustainability leaders, and policymakers.

title: Waiting for elective orthopaedic surgery: A qualitative scoping review of the patient experience
abstract: Public health waiting lists for elective or planned orthopaedic surgery are increasing to the point where demand far exceeds our ability to treat. This is largely due to ageing populations, rising obesity and the continued impact of delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. While waiting, patients suffer debilitating physical pain, functional limitation, social isolation and associated mental health impacts while some are unable to work. This qualitative scoping review explored and mapped the experiences of patients of waiting for elective or planned orthopaedic surgery. This review was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute Scoping Review methodology and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews. A comprehensive database search was conducted to identify English language articles from 2009 until June 2025. Data extraction was informed by the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research. Results were thematically analysed and presented using the Quality Health Outcomes Model. The initial search identified 4713 articles, of which, 21 manuscripts met inclusion criteria. The 21 articles comprised 17 primary qualitative research studies and four review articles published within the designated time period (2009 to 2025). Two key themes were identified: 1. Patients waiting for elective orthopaedic surgery need psychosocial support and 2. System-level, multi-factorial communication issues with the waiting list leave patients feeling lost between primary and specialist care. These themes suggest that the challenges faced due to lengthy elective surgery waiting lists are not simply a capacity issue, but also a challenge of coordinated, patient- centred care. Waiting for surgery is consistently described by patients as a source of anxiety and distress. With waiting list times for elective surgery increasing, the experience can be improved in part with adequate communication from healthcare providers. A re-focus on what matters most to the patient and their family is required in order to deliver adequate patient-centred care while patients wait for surgery.

title: From Sparse Visits to Continuous Molecular Trajectories with Flow Matching
abstract: Longitudinal transcriptomic studies often capture only a few molecular snapshots of each patient over time. This makes it challenging to understand how patients are progressing, compare them when progression rates differ, and capture molecular changes between observed visits. We introduce CohortFM, a flow-matching framework that reconstructs continuous patient-specific molecular trajectories from sparse longitudinal observations and organizes them through an integrated mixture model into a compact set of cohort-level progression patterns. CohortFM separates molecular progression from calendar time, places patients on a shared progression scale, uses observed intermediate states to guide the learned trajectories, and maps the resulting patterns back to real patient samples for biological interpretation. We evaluated CohortFM across COVID-19, sepsis, influenza, and tuberculosis. Despite different sampling patterns, the method generalizes well and consistently produces meaningful trajectories. These trajectories capture biological differences between patients that cannot be explained by the observed samples alone. Compared with state-of-the-art trajectory baselines, CohortFM produces more biologically distinct trajectories and a more complete representation of the patient population. Its finer progression scale also reveals biological programs and temporal dynamics that are not captured by visit-level analysis. We further evaluated interpolation and true forward prediction to test whether CohortFM can accurately recover unobserved states. CohortFM remains competitive with strong interpolation baselines and is among the strongest learned predictors in the harder forecasting setting. Ablation experiments further show that flow matching is the core learning mechanism and that our design choices improve continuous trajectory learning. Our results support CohortFM as a practical framework for turning sparse molecular snapshots into continuous, biologically interpretable trajectories. By going beyond visit labels, CohortFM makes it possible to study disease progression and predict future molecular states even when patients are sampled only a few times.

title: Q Fever in the Russian Federation: Analysis of the Epidemiological and Epizootiological Situation, Problematic Issues
abstract: The aim of the review is to assess the Q fever situation in the Russian Federation based on official registration data and analysis of the epidemiological situation during 2013–2024, excluding the data for 2020 and 2021, the period of anti-epidemic measures to prevent COVID-19, and to determine the current aspects of the fight against this infection. The epidemic potential of Q fever in Russia and other countries, where an increase in the activity of its foci is observed, is evaluated. The regions of the Russian Federation with unfavorable Q fever status are ranked based on the incidence rates of registered cases. The incidence of Q fever in the Russian Federation in 2024 is analyzed and forecasts for 2025 are provided for affected territories. The paper presents an analysis of the results of Q fever monitoring in the Stavropol, Altai, Primorsky Territories, Astrakhan, Rostov and Omsk Regions in 2024. Proposals are made to clarify and stabilize the epidemiological situation on Q fever.

title: The impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the dynamics of cases of disability related to respiratory diseases in the provision of primary health care in Moscow
abstract: The high contagiousness and prevalence of diseases during the COVID-19 pandemic necessitated the creation of electronic and digital disability certificates, as well as the introduction and active use of telemedicine technologies in medical institutions. However, the contribution of COVID-19 to the structure of temporary disability rates in different regions and its comparison with similar rates in other territories has not been fully studied. The article provides a comparative analysis of cases, days, and the sex-age structure of temporary disability and their distribution by respiratory diseases in the period 2019—2024, as recorded in a medical organization providing primary healthcare in Moscow. The analysis of the presented data reveals a complex dynamic of disability cases, demonstrating significant variability throughout the period under review.

title: Viral triggers of Guillain-Barré syndrome: implications for laboratory diagnostics.
abstract: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is a leading cause of acquired acute neuromuscular paralysis and is an immune-mediated disorder of the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Accumulating evidence indi-cates that GBS is often preceded by infectious events that trigger autoimmune responses through mechanisms such as molecular mimicry and autoantibody production. Campylobacter jejuni remains the most common bacterial agent, but viral pathogens also contribute to the development of GBS. This review summarizes the current evidence regarding viruses as triggers of GBS, including herpes-viruses, hepatotropic viruses (A, B, C, and E), human immunodeficiency virus, Zika virus, influenza virus, varicella-zoster virus, and the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. Emphasis is placed on laboratory test results related to viral GBS, including antiganglioside antibodies, serological markers of recent in-fection, molecular diagnostic methods, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis. From the standpoint of la-boratory medicine, both the clinical diagnosis and the distinction of GBS subtypes can be supported by the identification of recent viral infections and the detection of immunological biomarkers. How-ever, cross-reactivity, extended antibody persistence, and inadequate assay standardization frequently make it difficult to interpret laboratory test results. In patients with probable viral GBS, this review shows the diagnostic significance and limitations of routine laboratory testing. It also highlights the significance of close coordination between laboratory professionals and clinicians.
