media_mentions.content_title: Heart Failure Mortality Before and After COVID-19: Demographic Variations and Urbanization Patterns in the United States (2018-2023)
media_mentions.content: Abstract Background: Contemporary evidence on heart failure (HF) recorded as the underlying cause of death remains fragmented across demographic groups and levels of urbanization. The 2018-2023 interval includes two years before the emergence of COVID-19 (2018-2019) and four years after its emergence (2020-2023). Objective: We aim to characterize the national underlying cause of HF mortality among US adults aged 45 years or older from 2018 through 2023; describe differences by sex, age, race, and Hispanic origin; and quantify changes in absolute death counts across the six National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) urbanization categories. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that the national age-adjusted HF mortality rate would increase and that demographic differences and variation in geographic death counts would persist. Methods: This retrospective, population-based, serial cross-sectional study used Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) Underlying Cause of Death data (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) I50). Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) per 100,000 were evaluated overall and across demographic groups; age-specific crude rates were used for age groups. Zero-joinpoint log-linear models estimated annual percent change (APC) for the overall population, race categories, and Hispanic-origin categories. Race and Hispanic origin were analyzed separately and may overlap. Urbanization analyses used death counts and percentage changes; urbanization-specific population-adjusted rates were not estimated. Deaths listing HF only as a contributing cause were outside the case definition. Results: There were 512,960 deaths with HF as the underlying cause; the aggregate AAMR was 59.6 per 100,000. No statistically significant overall temporal trend was detected (APC: 0.59%; 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.37 to 1.57; p = 0.227). Men had a higher aggregate AAMR than women (68.1 versus 53.0), and Black adults had the highest racial AAMR (70.9). Asian adults had a lower aggregate AAMR than White and Black adults (22.9); Hispanic adults had a lower AAMR than non-Hispanic adults (35.2 versus 61.9). In their respective analyses, Asian and Hispanic groups had increasing trends at the nominal 0.05 significance level (APC: 1.30%, p = 0.047, and 1.96%, p = 0.030, respectively). Age-specific mortality increased sharply with age. Death counts increased across all six urbanization categories, most in Medium Metro counties (+11.0%). Conclusions: No statistically significant national trend was detected during 2018-2023, while descriptive demographic differences and nominally significant increases in the Asian race and Hispanic-origin analyses were observed. These separate analyses do not establish differences between subgroup slopes or narrowing mortality gaps. Geographic findings describe absolute burden, not population-adjusted risk. The results concern HF as the underlying cause and do not measure total HF-associated mortality. Introduction Heart failure (HF) represents a major and growing public health burden in the United States because of its high prevalence, mortality, recurrent hospitalization, and healthcare utilization. Approximately 7.7 million US adults were living with HF in 2021-2023, and 89,795 deaths were attributable to HF in 2023 [1]. This burden is expected to increase with population aging and the rising prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors; HF prevalence is projected to increase from 2.7% in 2020 to 3.8% by 2050 [2]. Although HF-related mortality declined during the early 2000s, this favorable trend slowed and subsequently reversed. National analyses using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) have documented increasing HF-related mortality after approximately 2011-2012, including among older and middle-aged adults, with additional perturbation during the COVID-19 era [3-8]. These observations make the 2018-2023 interval epidemiologically informative because it includes 2018-2019 before the emergence of COVID-19 and 2020-2023 after its emergence. These calendar-year descriptions do not define mutually exclusive pandemic phases or constitute a formal pre/post comparison. The mortality burden has not been distributed uniformly. Prior studies have documented differences by sex, race and ethnicity, geographic region, and urbanization, with higher population-adjusted HF mortality reported among men, non-Hispanic Black adults, and many rural populations [3,4,6-9]. Some prior studies have reported lower aggregate mortality in selected Hispanic-origin and Asian race comparisons. A Florida ecological analysis reported an inverse association between Hispanic population concentration and cardiovascular mortality [10]; that area-level finding does not establish individual protection or explain national HF-specific mortality. Similarly, Siddiqi et al. demonstrated that Asian American adults consistently maintained the lowest heart failure-related mortality rates among older US adults prior to the pandemic [5]. Contemporary underlying-cause HF mortality trends among adults aged 45 years or older in these population groups merit further description. Race and Hispanic origin are separate classifications, so these groups may overlap and should not be treated as mutually exclusive cohorts. Potential explanations include differences in cardiovascular risk-factor burden, socioeconomic conditions, continuity of care, medication access, specialist availability, and other social determinants of health [9,11,12]. Because these factors are not measured in aggregate mortality files, however, they should be used to contextualize rather than causally explain observed subgroup differences. Contemporary evidence nevertheless remains fragmented. Several national analyses ended in 2018-2021 or focused on selected age groups [3,5,8], whereas more recent studies extending through 2022-2023 examined middle-aged adults or place of death [4,13]. In addition, many prior studies combined HF listed as an underlying or contributing cause of death, an approach that captures a broader but conceptually different mortality burden. Underlying-cause HF mortality during 2018-2023 therefore remains incompletely characterized across multiple demographic dimensions and the full National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) urban-rural continuum within a single national analysis. The primary objective of this study was to characterize national trends in mortality attributable to HF as the underlying cause of death among US adults aged 45 years or older from 2018 through 2023. Secondary objectives were to quantify differences by sex, age, race, Hispanic origin, and race-by-sex strata; to evaluate prespecified temporal trends using joinpoint regression; and to describe changes in the absolute number of HF deaths across the six NCHS urbanization categories as a description of geographic burden rather than population-adjusted mortality risk. We hypothesized that the national age-adjusted mortality rate (AAMR) would increase over the study period and that demographic rate differences and variation in geographic death counts would persist. Materials & Methods Study design and period This retrospective, population-based, serial cross-sectional trend study examined mortality attributable to HF among US adults aged 45 years and older for a prespecified analytic period from 2018 through 2023. The study is ecological and descriptive; associations observed across population strata were not interpreted as individual-level causal effects. Data source Mortality data were obtained from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) Underlying Cause of Death, 2018-2024, Single Race database [14]. The database compiles de-identified death-certificate data for residents of all 50 US states and the District of Columbia. Cause of death is coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) [15]. Study population and inclusion/exclusion criteria The study population comprised US resident decedents aged 45 years or older. Deaths were included if the death occurred between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2023, inclusive, and the death certificate listed an ICD-10 code within the I50 category as the underlying cause of death. Decedents younger than 45 years, deaths of non-US residents, and deaths outside the 50 states and District of Columbia were excluded. Records with unknown demographic values were excluded from stratum-specific rate comparisons when a valid population denominator was unavailable. Data collection and variable definitions The primary outcome was a death for which ICD-10 category I50 was selected as the underlying cause. This is a cause-specific death-certificate endpoint, not all-cause mortality among people with HF and not all deaths involving HF. Deaths in which HF appeared only as a contributing cause were not included; thus, this analysis captures a subset of the broader HF-associated mortality burden. The complete I50 category in the CDC WONDER Underlying Cause of Death database includes I50.0 (congestive heart failure), I50.1 (left ventricular failure), and I50.9 (heart failure, unspecified). For most stratified extractions, cases were identified using CDC WONDER's predefined "Heart failure (I50)" category. A separate query selecting I50.0, I50.1, and I50.9 individually was used to characterize the distribution of HF subtype coding. Age was grouped as 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75-84, and 85 years or older. Sex was categorized as female or male as recorded on the death certificate. Race was categorized using the CDC WONDER Single-Race six-category classification: White; Black or African American; American Indian or Alaska Native; Asian; Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander; and more than one race. Hispanic origin was analyzed separately as Hispanic or Latino, Not Hispanic or Latino, or Not Stated. Each race category includes persons of any Hispanic origin, and each Hispanic-origin category includes persons of any race. Race and Hispanic origin therefore constitute separate, potentially overlapping analytic groupings, not mutually exclusive cohorts. Race and sex were additionally cross-classified to describe AAMRs across race-by-sex strata. These cross-classified comparisons were descriptive and were not treated as a formal statistical interaction test. County of residence was classified using the 2013 NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme for Counties: Large Central Metro, Large Fringe Metro, Medium Metro, Small Metro, Micropolitan, and Noncore [16]. All six categories were retained to describe the distribution of absolute HF mortality burden across the full urban-rural continuum. The selected Single-Race queries did not supply the denominators needed for the urbanization analyses. WONDER documents limitations for county/urbanization rates with 10-year age groups and for its standard county-level age-adjusted rates; five-year-age population queries can be available in other configurations. In addition, national urbanization queries including Connecticut have denominator limitations from 2022 onward [14]. The restriction here is specific to the query structure and period, rather than universal suppression of all geographic populations. Accordingly, the urbanization analysis in this study was restricted to absolute death counts and percentage change, calculated as 100 × (deaths in 2023 - deaths in 2018) / deaths in 2018. An external-denominator analysis would require harmonized age groups, population-estimate vintages, and county boundaries; no such alternative rate analysis was performed. No population-adjusted urbanization-specific mortality rates were estimated, and geographic findings were not interpreted as differences in mortality risk or access to care. Data were extracted directly from the CDC WONDER online query system using the Underlying Cause of Death, 2018-2024, Single Race database, with all results filtered to 2018-2023. The cause-of-death filter included I50.0, I50.1, and I50.9. Age was restricted to 45 years or older. Separate queries were performed for the overall annual trend, sex, race, Hispanic origin, race-by-sex strata, age group, and the 2013 six-level urbanization classification, as well as selected combinations such as year by race and year by Hispanic origin. Raw exports preserved CDC WONDER output designations including Suppressed, Unreliable, Not Applicable, and Not Available; these values were not replaced with zeros. Data extraction was performed independently by two analysts between August 10 and 12, 2026, using identical query parameters. The two extractions were compared only after completion, and discrepancies were resolved by re-querying CDC WONDER directly. A reconciled master dataset and data dictionary were then compiled. The US 2000 standard population was used for age adjustment. CDC WONDER-provided AAMRs were used for eligible overall and demographic groupings. Age-group results were reported as age-specific crude rates rather than AAMRs. For urbanization, only death counts and changes in counts were analyzed because the required denominators for age-adjusted rates were unavailable in the selected query structure. The principal mortality measure was the age-adjusted mortality rate (AAMR) per 100,000 population, standardized to the US 2000 standard population. Age-specific crude mortality rates per 100,000 were used for the predefined age groups. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals (CI) for age-adjusted rates followed CDC/NCHS methods, including the Fay-Feuer gamma approximation where applicable [17]. Rate ratios were calculated as the ratio of selected AAMRs, including the aggregate male-to-female comparison. Statistical analysis Temporal trends in AAMRs were evaluated using the National Cancer Institute Joinpoint Regression Program (version 5.2.0), with calendar year as the independent variable and the natural logarithm of the AAMR as the dependent variable [18]. Annual rate estimates and their standard errors were used in the trend analysis. Models for the overall population, six race categories, and two Hispanic-origin categories were prespecified with 0 joinpoints, yielding one log-linear segment over the six annual observations from 2018 to 2023. No change-point selection or inference about pandemic-specific inflection points was undertaken. Annual percent change (APC) was calculated as 100 × (exp(beta) - 1), where beta is the fitted annual slope. The reported 95% confidence intervals and p-values describe the APC estimates and the null hypothesis of zero temporal change; the nominal two-sided significance threshold was 0.05. Monte Carlo permutation testing for the selection of the number of joinpoints should not be confused with inference for a slope in a model fixed at 0 joinpoints. APC was the primary trend measure; AAPC was not separately reported because there was only one segment. Sex, age, and race-by-sex comparisons remained descriptive. No formal between-group slope comparison or interaction test was performed, so significance in one group and nonsignificance in another does not establish a difference between their trends. Subgroup p-values are interpreted as nominal, exploratory evidence rather than definitive proof of differential trends. No additional sex-, age-, or race-by-sex trend models or sensitivity analysis excluding 2020-2021 were performed for this revision. Excluding those two years would leave only four observations (2018, 2019, 2022, and 2023), with a two-year internal gap, limiting a stable assessment of whether trends persist outside the pandemic-associated fluctuations. This does not demonstrate robustness to exclusion of pandemic years. Cause-of-death misclassification is possible because HF is a common terminal pathway for multiple cardiovascular and noncardiovascular conditions and death-certificate detail varies across certifiers. Restricting the analysis to HF as the underlying cause of death may therefore underestimate the broader contribution of HF to mortality. Race and Hispanic-origin classifications on death certificates may differ from Census-derived population denominators, with potentially greater misclassification in some smaller racial groups. The ecological design also precludes individual-level inference because CDC WONDER does not provide patient-level clinical, treatment, insurance, or socioeconomic information. Finally, suppression and unreliability rules may reduce precision in smaller subgroups, particularly in finely stratified analyses. CDC WONDER suppresses death counts of fewer than 10 to protect confidentiality. Rates flagged by CDC WONDER as unreliable were not treated as valid numeric estimates. Under current NCHS presentation standards [19], rates based on fewer than 10 deaths are suppressed, and estimates based on 10 or more deaths may also be withheld when the relative width of the appropriate 95% confidence interval exceeds 160%; analogous criteria apply to age-adjusted rates using the Fay-Feuer confidence interval. Suppressed or unreliable cells were excluded from rate calculations and were not imputed. This study used publicly available, de-identified, aggregate mortality data and did not involve identifiable individual patient information. The analysis therefore did not constitute human-subject research requiring institutional review board oversight under the usual interpretation of US federal regulations governing research with publicly available de-identified data. All data used in this study are publicly available through CDC WONDER [14].
